title: Symphony No. 4 in B-flat major
hook: The sunny symphony between the Eroica and the Fifth, which begins in darkness and ends laughing.

painting.title: Portrait of Juliette Récamier
painting.pairingNote: Painted a few years before the symphony, Juliette Récamier sits in a white dress in the Greek fashion of the day; Schumann is said to have called the Fourth “a slender Greek maiden between two Norse giants”.

facts: Beethoven spent the summer of 1806 at the Silesian estate of his patron Prince Lichnowsky. In September they visited Count Franz von Oppersdorff, who kept a private orchestra and played Beethoven’s Second Symphony for him. The count then paid for a new symphony, and Beethoven wrote this one, dedicating it to him.

He had already begun the Fifth, but set it aside. Why the commission became this lighter, more Haydn-like work instead is not known; one suggestion is that the count’s liking for the Second invited something in the same vein.
It was first played privately in March 1807 at the Vienna palace of Prince Lobkowitz, and in public at the Burgtheater in April 1808.

It has always lived in the shadow of its neighbours. Schumann is said to have called it “a slender Greek maiden between two Norse giants”; Berlioz wrote that the slow movement seemed the work of the Archangel Michael rather than of a human being.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a dark, hushed introduction that bursts into high spirits (I), a slow song over a steady heartbeat (II), a dance that keeps tripping over its own beat (III), and a perpetual-motion finale that ends with a joke (IV).

movements.heading: Adagio – Allegro vivace
movements.summary: The symphony begins almost in the dark: a soft, low note, a long-held chord in the winds, and strings creeping downwards in the minor, as if the music cannot find its key. After thirty-eight slow bars, loud chords break the spell and the music races off in high spirits. The fast part is a [[sonata-form|sonata form]], with a famous hushed drum roll leading back to the main theme.

mainIdeas.name: The introduction
mainIdeas.description: quiet, slow, uncertain, wandering through distant keys.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1
mainIdeas.description: a quick, springing tune that shoots upwards.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2
mainIdeas.description: a little “conversation between the bassoon, the oboe and the flute” (Tovey).

stops.hear: A single soft plucked note, a held chord in the winds, and strings slowly creeping downwards
stops.happening: The slow introduction, in B-flat minor rather than major

stops.hear: The music gathers itself; loud, repeated chords from the whole orchestra
stops.happening: The end of the introduction, building to the Allegro

stops.hear: A quick, springing tune races upwards in the violins
stops.happening: The Allegro vivace: theme 1, in the home key at last

stops.hear: A light, playful tune passed from bassoon to oboe to flute
The springing tune again, from the start
The themes are broken up and pushed into far-off keys
Everything goes quiet; a soft drum roll rumbles while the strings feel their way back
stops.happening: The famous [[pedal-note|pedal note]] on the timpani, preparing the return

stops.hear: A crescendo, and the whole orchestra bursts back in with the main theme

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: A lively, determined close

notice: Compare the first minute with the moment the Allegro starts. The same symphony goes from groping in the dark to sprinting in the sun in a few seconds.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Carlos Kleiber recorded very little in the studio, and this is a live concert from the Nationaltheater in Munich, given on 3 May 1982. The Fourth was one of his favourite works: nine recordings of it by him are known. On the Spotify album a fifth track holds the audience’s applause, which is not part of the symphony.

movements.heading: Adagio
movements.summary: A long, slow song in E-flat. Under it, from the first bar to the last, runs a steady figure of a long and a short note, like a quiet heartbeat. The song returns several times, more richly decorated each time, and between its returns the clarinet sings a second, still gentler melody. At the very end the timpani play the heartbeat alone.

mainIdeas.name: The heartbeat
mainIdeas.description: a long–short figure, first in the second violins.

mainIdeas.name: The song
mainIdeas.description: a broad, tender melody in the first violins.

mainIdeas.name: The second melody
mainIdeas.description: a soft, singing tune for solo clarinet.

stops.hear: A gentle, rocking long–short figure, then the violins sing a broad, slow melody over it
stops.happening: The heartbeat and the main song

stops.hear: The clarinet sings a soft, tender melody
The main song returns, now decorated with many small notes
A darker passage, louder and in the minor
Calm again; the song comes back, now in the flute
stops.happening: The main theme, varied once more

stops.hear: The clarinet’s melody returns

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: The timpani alone tap out the long–short heartbeat; two soft chords close

notice: Keep an ear on the long–short figure. It passes through almost every instrument, and in the last bars only the drums are left playing it.

movements.heading: Allegro vivace – Un poco meno allegro
movements.tempo: Allegro vivace – Un poco meno allegro
movements.summary: Many scores call it a minuet, but it is far too fast to dance to: a [[scherzo|scherzo]] whose tune keeps pulling against its own three-beat bar, so that the music seems to stumble in twos. Its gentler middle section, the [[trio|trio]], comes round twice, and the main section three times, a lay-out Beethoven used again in the Seventh Symphony. At the end two horns blow the movement away.

mainIdeas.name: The scherzo
mainIdeas.description: loud, jabbing phrases whose accents fall in twos across the three beats, a kind of [[hemiola|hemiola]].

mainIdeas.name: The trio
mainIdeas.description: slower, quiet woodwind phrases, with the violins chirping in between.

stops.hear: Loud, jerky phrases that seem to limp across the beat
A gentler, slower tune in the woodwind, with little interjections from the violins
The jerky dance returns
The woodwind tune again

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The dance a third time, shortened; then the two horns call out, and the movement is over

notice: Try tapping three beats to a bar in the opening section. Within seconds Beethoven’s accents will throw you off.

movements.heading: Allegro ma non troppo
movements.summary: A finale in non-stop motion, a [[perpetuum-mobile|perpetuum mobile]] of quick notes passed around the orchestra, full of jokes and sudden contrasts. Beethoven called this mood *aufgeknöpft*, “unbuttoned”. Near the end, in Haydn’s manner, he brings back the main tune at half speed, broken by pauses, before a last rush.

mainIdeas.name: The main theme
mainIdeas.description: a whirl of fast notes in the violins.

mainIdeas.name: The bassoon
mainIdeas.description: in the return of the theme, the first bassoon has to play the whirling notes alone, a passage bassoonists know well.

stops.hear: The violins whirl off in fast, continuous notes; loud chords answer
A smoother tune in the woodwind, over the busy strings
The whirling theme from the start
The music turns stormier, the fast notes tossed between sections
The bassoon alone races through the fast theme
stops.happening: The [[recapitulation|recapitulation]] begins with the bassoon solo

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: The main tune slowed down, with pauses, then a sudden loud dash to the end
stops.happening: The joke ending: the theme at half speed, then the final flourish

notice: Listen for the bassoon around three minutes. The fast notes that the violins whirled through at the start are now given to one wind player, unaccompanied.

threads.title: Darkness to light, briefly
threads.body: The symphony opens in hushed uncertainty, but the darkness lasts only a minute and a half. Everything after is light, fast and witty.

threads.title: Haydn’s shadow
threads.body: The slow introduction, the wit, the pauses before the end all recall Haydn, Beethoven’s former teacher, still alive when the Fourth was first played.

threads.title: The timpani
threads.body: The soft drum roll in the first movement, the drum heartbeat at the end of the Adagio: Beethoven gives the timpani quiet, important moments, not only loud ones.
